title: LLM API Battlecard: Fast-Fallback Positioning Playbook
content:
Executive summary:

Short take: For engineering-first buyers who care about predictable latency, cost per token, and production reliability, Redwood shifts the conversation from "which model" to "how inference is served". Against generic LLM API providers (large public APIs and cloud-hosted model endpoints), our core win is: deterministic economics + operational controls + multi-environment parity (hosted, dedicated, private).

Why this matters to buyers:
- Startups: want low-latency experience and predictable monthly burn as usage scales.
- Platform teams: need rollout controls, tracing, and consistent SLAs across business units.
- Regulated customers: need VPC/on-prem options, key management, and auditability.

Positioning frame (elevator lines):
- For engineering teams building customer-facing LLM features, Redwood is the inference runtime that guarantees production-grade latency, transparent unit economics, and unified tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — so you don’t outgrow your API.
- Against simple LLM APIs: they give model access. We give sustainable production serving.

Competitor snapshot (high-level):
- Large public LLM APIs (A): Excellent model breadth and rapid model launches. Weakness: opaque unit economics for high-throughput workloads, limited private deployment options, limited ability to control batching/quantization or routing.
- Cloud vendor managed endpoints (B): Tight cloud integration and enterprise SLAs, but often higher baseline ops costs, less inference-optimized runtimes, and patchy multi-region fallbacks.
- Specialist inference vendors (C): Good performance in narrow cases but typically require heavy integration, custom ops, and lack our unified model/version rollout and hosted fallback story.

Feature comparison (talking points, not a full table):
- Latency SLOs: Redwood -> explicit SLOs + can show token-level latency breakdowns. Competitors -> model-dependent, often no per-route SLOs.
- Cost transparency: Redwood -> per-route cost breakout and recommendations (batching, quantization). Competitors -> per-token billing but opaque where costs accumulate (cache misses, retries).
- Dedicated capacity & predictable throughput: Redwood Dedicated -> reserved GPU pools and burst controls. Public APIs -> subject to throttles and noisy neighbors.
- Private/VPC options: Redwood Private -> full private control plane + on-prem option. Many public APIs -> no air-gapped option.
- Observability & rollouts: Redwood -> per-model dashboards, canary/A-B rollouts, automatic fallback policies. Competitors -> minimal rollout controls or DIY.
- Model quality tradeoffs: We support model variants + deterministic fallback routing to avoid user-visible regressions when capacity or cost constraints hit.

Common sales traps and how to avoid them (what to watch for):
- Trap: Prospect believes cheaper per-token equals cheaper overall.
  - Reality: Latency, retries, cache patterns, and throughput multiply cost. Use a 30-day cost projection to show unit economics under their traffic pattern.
- Trap: Prospect defaults to choosing the newest/biggest model.
  - Reality: Not every use case needs SOTA; recommend smaller quantized variants and show quality vs cost trade-offs with example prompts.
- Trap: Prospect assumes cloud native automatically means lower ops cost.
  - Reality: Without inference-optimized runtimes and rollout/control tooling there is hidden SRE tax. Use our console screenshots showing reduced incident MTTR and rollout velocity.

Objection handling (scripted responses):
- Objection: "We use Provider X for model access; switching is costly."
  - Response: "We typically integrate at the API layer in under 2 weeks for the core use-case. For data/control requirements we provide Dedicated and Private paths. Show them our migration checklist and a staging runbook."
- Objection: "OpenAI/BigCloud has better models."
  - Response: "Model quality moves fast — we support a curated catalog of open and proprietary variants and make it easy to benchmark them. Crucially, we optimize how those models are served so you get consistent latency and lower per-token costs in production."
- Objection: "Why not just self-host?"
  - Response: "Self-hosting means building an inference runtime, autoscaling, KV cache management, and observability. Redwood is that stack as a managed and private option — we reduce time to production and operational overhead while giving you control if you want it."

Demo and proof points (what to show on a call):
- Live console: per-route token/latency/cost breakdown for a real workload (or anonymized example).
- Canary rollback: trigger a canary, inject failure, show automatic fallback to compatible model variant.
- Cost regression example: show two strategies (no batching vs inferred batching) and the monthly delta at expected QPS.
- Dedicated throughput demo: synthetic load test showing predictable p99 latency under sustained load versus public API throttling.

Win themes (short bullets you should repeat):
- Predictable economics: not just per-token pricing, but unit economics under real traffic.
- Production-first: rollouts, tracing, fallback, SLAs.
- One API, many runtimes: same integration for hosted, dedicated, and private.

Discovery playbook (questions to ask early):
- What does your current QPS and peak look like? any seasonality?
- Which routes are latency-critical vs best-effort?
- What allowances do you have for model quantization / smaller variants?
- Do you require VPC/on-prem or specific KMS/HSM integrations?
- Who owns incident response? Is MTTR a metric you track?

Competitive traps to deploy tactically (sales nudges):
- Ask them about retrospective cost surprises — owners often concede they saw unexpected spend spikes. Use it as an opening to show Redwood's cost transparency.
- If they love a specific model vendor, pivot to multi-model serving: show how Redwood can use that vendor for quality experiments while controlling routing and fallback in prod.

Appendix: Quick rebut templates (one-liners)
- "We want best model quality": "We help you run SOTA experiments while ensuring production economics don't blow up."
- "We already have an account with X": "Great — we can sit in front or beside it and immediately start reducing unit costs and adding SLAs."
- "It's cheaper to run in-house": "If you have 6–9 months and full SRE focus, maybe — otherwise realize the ops and regression cost we eliminate in weeks."

Next steps (internal):
- Finalize cost projection templates for the most common prospect archetypes (SaaS chat, search/rerank, embeddings-heavy analytics).
- Create 2 demo recordings tailored to Platform and Startup buyer archetypes.
- Coordinate with Applied ML to keep 3 benchmark prompts current for model-quality trade-offs.

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- We should add a small side-by-side quantization example (4-bit vs 8-bit) with latency and quality numbers from recent benchmarks.
- Pull the Dedicated capacity SLO doc into Confluence and link in the public demo.

(Informal draft: intended to be a living battlecard — feel free to chop, add competitor-specific numbers, and iterate.)
